For further details, please review the full disclaimer available on the platform. 6. The FDA package insert for Welchol tablets does not include any Black Box Warnings. 7. Welchol is classified as an anti-anginal, antiarrhythmic, and beta-adrenergic blocker. It is FDA-approved for the treatment of acute myocardial infarction, angina, and hypertension. 8. Common adverse reactions associated with Welchol include bradyarrhythmia, heart block, heart failure, hypotension, pruritus, rash, constipation, diarrhea, indigestion, nausea, dizziness, fatigue, headache, depression, dyspnea, and wheezing. 9. For primary hyperlipidemia in adults, Welchol is indicated as an adjunct to diet and exercise to reduce elevated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C). It can be used as monotherapy or in combination with HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors (statins). 10. In pediatric patients aged 10 to 17 years with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, Welchol is indicated to reduce LDL-C levels when dietary therapy alone is insufficient, provided LDL-C levels remain ≥190 mg/dL or ≥160 mg/dL with additional cardiovascular risk factors. 11. Lipid-altering agents, including Welchol, should be used alongside a diet low in saturated fat and cholesterol when non-pharmacological interventions are inadequate. 12. In patients with coronary heart disease (CHD) or CHD risk equivalents such as diabetes mellitus, LDL-C treatment goals are prioritized. If triglycerides (TG) exceed 200 mg/dL, non-HDL cholesterol becomes a secondary target. 13. For type 2 diabetes mellitus, Welchol is indicated as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control. The recommended dosage is six tablets once daily or three tablets twice daily. 14. Welchol is not indicated for the treatment of type 1 diabetes or diabetic ketoacidosis. It has not been extensively studied in combination with dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors or thiazolidinediones. 15. Welchol has not been studied in pediatric patients with type 2 diabetes, in children younger than 10 years, or in pre-menarcheal girls. 16. Welchol is contraindicated in patients with a history of bowel obstruction, serum triglyceride concentrations >500 mg/dL, or a history of hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis. 17. Welchol may increase serum triglyceride levels. Lipid parameters, including TG levels, should be assessed before initiating therapy and monitored periodically thereafter. 18. If TG levels exceed 500 mg/dL or if hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis develops, Welchol should be discontinued. 19. Bile acid sequestrants like Welchol may reduce the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K). Patients on vitamin supplementation should take their vitamins at least four hours before Welchol. 20. Due to its constipating effects, Welchol is not recommended for patients with gastroparesis, other gastrointestinal motility disorders, or those at risk for bowel obstruction. 21. Welchol tablets may cause dysphagia or esophageal obstruction due to their size. Patients with swallowing disorders should use the oral suspension form. 22. To avoid esophageal distress, Welchol for oral suspension should always be mixed with water, fruit juice, or diet soft drinks before ingestion. 23. Welchol reduces gastrointestinal absorption of certain drugs. Medications with known interactions should be administered at least four hours prior to Welchol. 24. In pregnancy, Welchol is classified as Category B. While animal studies have shown no evidence of fetal harm, its use during pregnancy should be limited to cases where it is clearly needed. 25. Welchol is not systemically absorbed and is not expected to be excreted in human milk. 26. The safety and efficacy of Welchol in children aged 10 to 17 years with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia have been evaluated. No significant effects on growth, sexual maturation, or fat-soluble vitamin levels were observed. 27. Welchol has not been studied in elderly patients with severe renal insufficiency (CrCl <30 mL/min). No dosage adjustments are required for patients with hepatic impairment. 28. Welchol therapy involves mixing the contents of a packet with water, fruit juice, or diet soft drinks. It should be taken with meals and not in its dry form. 29. Welchol is a non-absorbed, lipid-lowering polymer that binds bile acids in the intestine, reducing their reabsorption. This process increases hepatic demand for cholesterol, leading to enhanced clearance of LDL-C from the blood. 30. The mechanism by which Welchol improves glycemic control in type 2 diabetes is not fully understood. However, its therapeutic effects on lipid levels are typically observed within two weeks of initiation. 31. Welchol is not metabolized systemically and does not interfere with systemic drug-metabolizing enzymes such as cytochrome P-450. 32. In clinical trials, Welchol therapy resulted in a median placebo-corrected increase in serum triglycerides of 5% to 22%, depending on the combination therapy used. 33. No cases of acute pancreatitis associated with hypertriglyceridemia were reported in clinical trials involving Welchol. 34. The long-term effects of hypertriglyceridemia on coronary artery disease risk remain uncertain. Caution is advised when treating patients with baseline triglyceride levels >300 mg/dL. 35. In clinical studies, Welchol demonstrated no significant differences in safety or efficacy between elderly and younger patients. However, greater sensitivity in some older individuals cannot be ruled out. 36. Welchol has not been shown to reduce the risk of macrovascular disease in patients with diabetes or hyperlipidemia. 37. Overdoses of Welchol have not been tested. However, excessive doses may cause severe gastrointestinal effects such as constipation.
